Title: Ashitey and Another v Dodoo [1967] GHACA 8 (13 March 1967)

Source: https://ghalii.org/akn/gh/judgment/ghaca/1967/8/eng@1967-03-13

Text: An infant was injured when struck by a lorry driven by the second defendant and owned (in form) by the first defendant. At trial the driver was found negligent and the judge held both defendants jointly and severally liable, apparently relying on ownership and consent. On appeal the defendants argued that ownership alone did not establish liability and that the trial judge should have found whether the driver was servant or agent. The Court of Appeal distinguished claims based on statutory breach under the Motor Vehicles (Third Party Insurance) Act, 1958 from negligence claims, noting there was no evidence the driver was uninsured so the statutory‑breach principle (Monk v Warbey) could not support owner’s personal liability. Ownership is only prima facie evidence of a servant/agent relationship. Exercising its power under rules 31 and 32, the court reheard the case on the record and concluded the ‘‘work and pay’’ arrangement (earnings paid to owner; licence and insurance in owner’s name; owner paid repairs, gave instructions and could seize vehicle) established control and joint interest, making the driver the servant/agent. The appeal was dismissed and the trial judgment against both defendants upheld.

Issues:
- Whether the owner of a motor vehicle can be held liable to a third party merely by virtue of ownership when another person negligently drives the vehicle?
- Whether an owner's liability to a third party can be founded on breach of the Motor Vehicles (Third Party Insurance) Act, 1958 where there is no evidence that the driver was uninsured?
- Whether the fact of ownership is conclusive or only prima facie evidence that the vehicle was being driven by the owner’s servant or agent?
- Whether a ‘‘work and pay’’ arrangement establishes that the driver was the servant or agent of the owner, rendering both jointly and severally liable?
- Whether the Court of Appeal may rehear the whole case and substitute the judgment of the trial court under rules 31 and 32 of the Supreme Court Rules, 1962?

Held:
- The court held that the trial judge would have erred if he based the owner’s personal liability on a statutory breach under the Motor Vehicles (Third Party Insurance) Act, 1958, because there was no evidence the driver was uninsured; the plaintiff’s claim was for negligence, not for breach of a statutory duty. The Monk v. Warbey principle therefore did not apply in the absence of proof of no insurance.
- The court held that ownership of a vehicle is only prima facie evidence that the vehicle was being driven by the owner or by his servant or agent; ownership alone does not automatically impose liability on the owner for the torts of a driver.
- Applying the court’s supervisory power under rules 31 and 32 of the Supreme Court Rules, 1962, the Court of Appeal reheard the case on the record and found on a fair view of the evidence that the ‘‘work and pay’’ system established sufficient control and joint interest to characterise the driver as servant or agent of the owner.
- Accordingly, the court held that on the proved facts (earnings paid to owner, licence and insurance in owner’s name, owner paid repairs, gave instructions and had a right to seize the vehicle) both owner and driver were jointly and severally liable for the negligence of the driver.

Title: Royal Exchange Assurance v Owusu [1965] GHASC 50 (21 June 1965)

Source: https://ghalii.org/akn/gh/judgment/ghasc/1965/50/eng@1965-06-21

Text: The respondent obtained judgment against the insured and the insured’s driver for injuries suffered when the insured’s car ran into a ditch. The respondent then sued the insurer under section 10(1) of the Motor Vehicles (Third Party Insurance) Act, 1958, to recover the judgment sum. The relevant policy covered private use (social, domestic, pleasure) and the insured’s business but expressly excluded use for hire or reward. The insurer denied liability on the ground that the car was being used for reward at the time of the accident. The Supreme Court held that section 10(1) permits recovery from an insurer only where (1) a judgment exists against an insured, (2) the judgment is for a liability required to be insured, and (3) the policy in fact covers the liability (or would but for avoidance/cancellation). The Court found that the respondent had been travelling as a passenger for reward, that the exclusion for hire or reward placed the use outside the policy, and that the claimant bore the onus of proving the vehicle’s use fell within the policy. Section 8 did not invalidate the exclusion. The insurer’s appeal was allowed.

Issues:
- Whether a person who obtains judgment against the insured for injuries caused by a motor vehicle may sue the insurer under section 10(1) of the Motor Vehicles (Third Party Insurance) Act, 1958, and what conditions must be satisfied for such a claim.
- Whether a policy condition excluding use of the motor-car for hire or reward is effective to defeat a third‑party claim under section 10(1) of the Act.
- Who bears the onus of proof on the issue whether the vehicle was being used in a manner that fell outside the scope of the insurer’s policy.
- Whether the absence of express authority by the insured for the driver to use the car for reward prevents the insurer from relying on the policy exclusion.
- Whether section 8 of the Motor Vehicles (Third Party Insurance) Act, 1958, invalidates policy terms that limit cover for third‑party risks such as an exclusion for hire or reward.

Held:
- The court held that three conditions must be fulfilled before an injured third party can recover from an insurer under section 10(1) of the Motor Vehicles (Third Party Insurance) Act, 1958: (1) the injured party must have obtained a judgment against a person insured by the policy; (2) that judgment must be in respect of a liability required to be covered by compulsory insurance under the Act; and (3) the terms of the policy actually cover the liability in question, or would have but for the insurer’s right to avoid or cancel the policy.
- On proper construction the policy in issue covered the insured’s private use (social, domestic and pleasure) and business use but expressly excluded use for hire or reward. The court held that carriage of the respondent as a passenger for reward placed the use outside the risk assumed by the insurers, so the policy did not cover the accident.
- The onus lay on the claimant (respondent) to prove that the relevant use of the vehicle did not put it outside the scope of the policy; it was erroneous for the trial judge to place that burden on the insurers.
- Express authority from the insured for the driver to use the car for reward was unnecessary. It was sufficient that the driver drove the car on the insured’s order or with his permission and that the driver was bound by the policy terms.
- Section 8 of the Act did not render the exclusion for hire or reward ineffective; section 8 addresses post‑accident conditions and does not invalidate conditions that circumscribe the operation of the policy from its commencement. Consequently there was no policy in force for the use in question and the insurers were not liable.

Title: Amegbor v Chahal and Another [1967] GHAHC 5 (17 May 1967)

Source: https://ghalii.org/akn/gh/judgment/ghahc/1967/5/eng@1967-05-17

Text: The plaintiff, a fare-paying passenger, was injured when a vehicle driven by a third person collided with a stationary obstacle; the vehicle was uninsured. The vehicle was held to be jointly owned under an arrangement by which the co‑owner had exclusive contractual possession and the right to use the vehicle for income‑earning purposes, and was responsible for insuring and maintaining it. The plaintiff sued one co‑owner (the other was untraceable) in tort for vicarious liability for the driver’s negligence and in statutory tort for breach of s.3(1) of the Motor Vehicles (Third Party Insurance) Act, 1958 (permitting uninsured use). The court found the driver negligent but on the evidence not to have been the defendant’s servant or agent; accordingly there was no vicarious liability. The court further held that where a joint‑ownership contract grants exclusive control to one joint‑owner, the other cannot be said to have ‘caused or permitted’ the use for purposes of s.3(1), and the plaintiff failed to prove he was deprived of recovery by reason of any statutory breach. A prior criminal plea of guilty by the defendant was admissible but of limited weight. The claim was dismissed and costs awarded to the defendant.

Issues:
- Whether a joint-owner can be vicariously liable in tort for the negligent driving of a servant or agent of his co-owner?
- Whether a joint-owner can be held in breach of the statutory duty to insure under Motor Vehicles (Third Party Insurance) Act, 1958 s.3(1), for permitting an uninsured vehicle to be used by his co-owner or the co-owner’s driver?
- What is the meaning and scope of ‘cause or permit’ (and of ‘permission’) under s.3(1) of the Motor Vehicles (Third Party Insurance) Act, 1958?
- What evidential weight, if any, does a plea of guilty to a related criminal charge have in subsequent civil proceedings arising from the same facts?

Held:
- On the facts, the driver who caused the accident was neither the servant nor the agent of the defendant; consequently the defendant was not vicariously liable in tort for the driver’s negligence.
- Where a contract creates joint ownership and confers on one joint-owner an exclusive contractual right to possess and use the vehicle for income‑earning purposes without any unilateral power in the other joint‑owner to control or forbid that use, the latter cannot be said to have ‘caused or permitted’ the use within s.3(1) of the Motor Vehicles (Third Party Insurance) Act, 1958. ‘Permission’ in that statutory context implies the unilateral power to forbid, regulate or limit use.
- To succeed under s.3(1) a plaintiff must prove (a) user not covered by insurance, (b) that the defendant caused or permitted that use, and (c) that the plaintiff suffered damage by reason of that breach — meaning the breach must have deprived the plaintiff of a realistic prospect of recovery from the primary wrongdoer. On the facts the plaintiff failed to show such damage attributable to the breach.
- A prior plea of guilty to a criminal charge admitting an uninsured user is admissible evidence but its weight is limited and depends on the circumstances in which it was made; a plea made for convenience or to avoid expense may carry little evidential value. In this case the court gave the plea little weight.
response:
The person responsible for the damage is normally the driver who caused the accident by driving carelessly — insurance only decides who ends up paying the money, not who is at fault.

In **Amegbor v Chahal and Another**, the court explained that under **section 3(1) of the Motor Vehicles (Third Party Insurance) Act, 1958**, it is an offence to let an uninsured vehicle be used on the road. But to succeed against someone on that basis, you must show three things: the vehicle truly had no insurance, that the person caused or allowed that uninsured use, and that the lack of insurance actually cost you the realistic chance of recovering from the driver. On those facts the claim failed — so the negligent driver himself stays personally responsible for your damage.

In **Ashitey and Another v Dodoo**, the court held that merely owning a vehicle is only on-the-face-of-it (prima facie) proof that the driver was driving for the owner. So if the car belongs to someone else who controls the driver, you may be able to pursue the owner too — but not based on ownership alone.

I also came across a Motor Compensation Fund in **section 250 of the Insurance Act, 2021**, but my documents don't explain how claims are made from it, so please ask a lawyer about that. Write down the driver's details, report to the police, and speak to a lawyer about suing the driver personally.

This is general information based on the documents I have, not formal legal advice. For your specific case, please speak to a lawyer or Legal Aid Ghana.

- Ashitey and Another v Dodoo [1967] GHACA 8 (13 March 1967) — https://ghalii.org/akn/gh/judgment/ghaca/1967/8/eng@1967-03-13
- Insurance Act, 2021 — https://ghalii.org/akn/gh/act/2021/1061/eng@2021-01-05#subpart_nn_56

Source: https://ghalii.org/akn/gh/act/1962/104/eng@1962-12-31#part_III

Text: 16. Effect on fit person orders Where an  adoption order  is made in respect of a  juvenile  in respect of whom a fit person’s order made by a Juvenile  Court  is in force, committing the  juvenile  to the care of any person, the fit person’s order shall cease to have effect. 17. Adopted Children Register (1) The Registrar-General shall maintain at the Office of the Registrar-General a register to be called the Adopted Children Register, in which shall be made such entries as may be directed to be made therein by adoption orders, but no other entries. (2) The Registrar-General may by executive instrument, make rules with respect to the Adopted Children Register and with respect to entries in the Register of Births relating to adopted persons and, in particular, rules— (a) for the admission in evidence of a certified copy of any entry in the Adopted Children Register; (b) as to searches in that Register and the fees to be charged in respect of the services made available in connection with that Register; (c) prescribing the form of the direction to be given in an  adoption order  as to making an entry in that Register, and the manner in which the making of an  adoption order  shall be communicated to the Registrar-General; (d) with respect to amendments and rectifications of the Adopted Children Register; and (e) for recording adoptions against entries in the Register of Births. (3) The Registrar-General shall, in addition to the Adopted Children Register, keep such other Registers and books, and make such entries therein, as may be necessary to record and make traceable the connection between any entry in the Register of Births which has been marked “ adopted ” in pursuance of rules under this section, and any corresponding entry in the Adopted Children Register, but the Registers and books kept under the provisions of this subsection shall not, nor shall any index thereof, be open to public inspection and search, nor, except under any order by the High  Court , shall the Registrar-General furnish any person with any information contained in, or with any copy or extract from, such Registers or books. 18. Prohibition of certain payments (1) It shall not be lawful for an adopter, or for a  parent  of a  juvenile , to receive, except with the sanction of the  Court , any payment or other reward in consideration of the adoption of the  juvenile  under this Act, or for any person to make or give or agree to make or give to an adopter, or  parent  any payment or reward the receipt of which is prohibited by this subsection. (2) It shall not be lawful for any person who is not the  parent  of a  juvenile  to receive or agree to receive any payment or other reward for making or facilitating any arrangements under which a  juvenile  is placed in the care and possession of a person who is also not the  parent  of the  juvenile , whether or not the arrangements  will  lead to the adoption of the  juvenile . (3) A person contravening this section shall be liable on summary conviction to imprisonment for a term not exceeding three months, or to a fine not exceeding one hundred pounds, or to both. 19. Restriction on sending juveniles abroad for adoption (1) Except under the authority of a licence issued under the next following section, it shall not be lawful for any person to permit, or to cause or procure, the care and possession of a  juvenile  to be transferred to a person who is resident outside Ghana and who is not the guardian or a  relative  of the  juvenile , if he knows or has reason to believe that the person to whom the care and possession of the  juvenile  is transferred has entered into any agreement or arrangements with a  parent  of the  juvenile  or with any other party which  will  or may lead to the adoption of the  juvenile  under the law of any country outside Ghana. (2) A person who contravenes the provisions of this section shall be liable on summary conviction to imprisonment for a term not exceeding six months or to a fine not exceeding fifty pounds or to both. 20. Licence to send  juvenile  abroad for adoption (1) Subject to the provisions of this section, the  Director  may grant a licence in the prescribed form, and subject to such conditions and restrictions as the  Director  thinks fit, authorising the care and possession of a  juvenile  for whose adoption arrangements have been made to be transferred to a person resident outside Ghana. (2) A licence shall not be granted under this section unless the  Director  is satisfied as respects every person whose consent would be required under section  3  of this Act to the making of an  adoption order  for the adoption of the  juvenile — (a) that the application is made with the consent of that person; or (b) that the consent of that person can properly be dispensed with on any ground on which the  Court  could dispense with a consent to an  adoption order  under the said section  3 . (3) A licence shall not be granted under this section unless the  Director  is satisfied that the person to whom the care and possession of the  juvenile  is proposed to be transferred is a suitable person to be entrusted therewith, and that the transfer is likely to be for the welfare of the  juvenile , due consideration being, for this purpose, given to the wishes of the  juvenile , having regard to the age and understanding of the  juvenile . 21. Interpretation In this Act, unless the context otherwise requires— “ adoption order ” means an order made under subsection  (1)  of section  1  of this Act; “ Court ” means a Court having jurisdiction to make adoption orders under this Act; “ Director ” means the Director of Social Welfare and Community Development; “ father ”, in relation to an illegitimate child, means the natural father; “ juvenile ” means a person who is under the age of seventeen years; “ parent ” includes a  father  as defined by this Act, and a guardian; “ relative ”, in relation to a  juvenile , means a grand- parent , brother, sister, uncle or aunt, or son or daughter of an uncle or aunt, whether of the full blood or half blood or by affinity, and includes— (a) where an  adoption order  has been made in respect of the  juvenile  or any other person, any person who would be a relative of the  juvenile  within the meaning of this definition if the adopted person were the child of the adopter born in lawful marriage; (b) where the  juvenile  is illegitimate, the  father  of the  juvenile  and any person who would be a relative of the  juvenile  within the meaning of this definition if the  juvenile  were the legitimate child of his mother and  father ; “ will ” includes any kind of testamentary disposition.

Title: Adoption Act, 1962

Source: https://ghalii.org/akn/gh/act/1962/104/eng@1962-12-31#part_I

Text: 1. Power to make adoption orders (1) Subject to the provisions of this Act, the  Court  may, upon an application made in the prescribed manner, make an order  authorising the applicant to adopt a  juvenile . (2) An  adoption order  may be made on the application of a man and his wife authorising them jointly to adopt a  juvenile . (3) An  adoption order  may be made authorising the adoption of a  juvenile  by the mother or  father  of the  juvenile , either alone or jointly with her husband or his wife as the case may be. 2. Restrictions on making adoption orders (1) An  adoption order  shall not be made unless   the applicant or, in the case of a joint application, one of the applicants— (a) has attained the age of twenty-five and is at least twenty-one years older than the  juvenile ; or (b) has attained the age of twenty-one and is a  relative  of the  juvenile ; or (c) is the mother or  father  of the  juvenile . (2) An  adoption order  shall not be made in favour of a sole applicant who is a male unless the  juvenile  is a son of the applicant or the  Court  is satisfied that there are special circumstances which justify as an exceptional measure the making of an  adoption order . (3) Except as provided by subsection  (2)  of section  3  of this Act, an  adoption order  shall not be made authorising more than one person to adopt a  juvenile . (4) An  adoption order  shall not be made in respect of a  juvenile  unless— (a) the applicant and the infant reside in Ghana; and (b) the  juvenile  has been continuously in the care and possession of the applicant for at least three consecutive months immediately preceding the date of the order; and (c) the applicant has, at least three months before the date of the order, notified the  Director  of his intention to apply for an  adoption order  in respect of the  juvenile . 3. Consent of parents to adoption (1) Subject to the provisions of this section, an  adoption order  shall not be made except with the consent of every person who is a  parent  of the  juvenile . (2) The  Court  may dispense with the consent of any  parent  of the  juvenile  if the  Court  is satisfied that he has abandoned, neglected or persistently illtreated the  juvenile , or that he cannot be found or is incapable of giving his consent or that his consent is unreasonably withheld. (3) If, in the case of an application made within one year from the date of the commencement of this Act, it is shown to the satisfaction of the  Court  that during the period of two years ending with that date the  juvenile  has been brought up, maintained and educated under any de facto adoption (whether by one person or by a husband and wife jointly) the  Court  may dispense with the consent of any  parent  of the  juvenile . (4) Any consent under this section may be given (either unconditionally or subject to conditions with respect to the religious persuasion in which the  juvenile  is to be brought up) without knowing the identity of the applicant for the  adoption order ; and where consent so given by any person is subsequently withdrawn on the ground only that he does not know the identity of the applicant, his consent shall be deemed for the purposes of this section to be unreasonably withheld. (5) While an application for an  adoption order  in respect of a  juvenile  is pending in any  Court , any  parent  of the  juvenile  who has signified his consent to the making of an  adoption order  in pursuance of the application shall not be entitled, except with the leave of the  Court , to remove the  juvenile  from the care and possession of the applicant; and in considering whether to grant or refuse such leave the  Court  shall have regard to the welfare of the  juvenile . 4. Other consents (1) Where it appears to the  Court  that any person who is not the  parent  of the  juvenile  has, under any order of a  Court  or agreement, or under customary law, or otherwise, any rights or obligations in respect of the  juvenile  the  Court  may, if they think fit, require that that person’s consent shall be obtained before the  adoption order  is made. (2) Where a married man or woman is the sole applicant for an  adoption order , the  Court  may, if they think fit, require that the consent of any wife or husband of the applicant be obtained before the  adoption order  is made. (3) It shall be the duty of the  Director  to prepare a report to assist the  Court  on an application for an  adoption order  to determine whether any person who is not a  parent  of the  juvenile  has any rights or obligations in respect of the  juvenile  and whether that person’s consent ought to be obtained to the  adoption order . 5. Functions of court as to adoption orders (1) The  Court  before making an  adoption order  shall be satisfied— (a) that every person whose consent is required under section  3  of this Act, and whose consent is not dispensed with, has consented to and understands the nature and effects of the  adoption order  for which the application is made, and in particular in the case of any  parent  understands that the effect of the  adoption order   will  be permanently to deprive him or her of his or her parental rights; (b) that the order if made  will  be for the welfare of the  juvenile , due consideration for this purpose being given to the wishes of the  juvenile  having regard to the age and understanding of the  juvenile ; and (c) that the applicant has not received or agreed to receive, and that no person has made or agreed to make to the applicant, any payment or other reward in consideration of the adoption except such as the  Court  may sanction. (2) The  Court  in an  adoption order  may impose such terms and conditions as the  Court  may think fit, and in particular may require the adopter by bond or otherwise to make for the  juvenile  such provision (if any) as in the opinion of the  Court  is just and expedient. 6. Interim orders (1) Subject to the provisions of this section, the  Court  may, upon any application for an  adoption order , postpone the determination of the application and make an interim order giving the custody of the  juvenile  to the applicant for a period not exceeding two years by way of a probationary period upon such terms as regards provision for the maintenance and education and supervision of the welfare of the  juvenile  and otherwise as the  Court  may think fit. (2) The  Court  shall impose as conditions under subsection  (1)  of this section— (a) that the  juvenile  shall be under the supervision of an officer appointed by the  Director , and (b) that the  juvenile  shall not be taken out of Ghana without the leave of the  Court . (3) All such consents as are required to an  adoption order  shall be necessary for an interim order but subject to a like power on the part of the  Court  to dispense with any such consent. (4) An interim order shall not be made in any case where the making of an  adoption order  would be unlawful by virtue of subsection  (4)  of section  2  of this Act. (5) An interim order shall not be deemed to be an  adoption order  within the meaning of this Act. 7. Application by a person who is not a citizen of Ghana Where the applicant or, in the case of a joint application, either of the applicants is not a citizen of Ghana the  Court  shall in exercise of their powers under the last foregoing section postpone the determination of the application and make an interim order for a period of not less than six months. 8. Children previously adopted An  adoption order  or an interim order may be made in respect of a  juvenile  who has already been the subject of an  adoption order  and the adopter under the previous adoption shall, if alive, be deemed to be the  parent  of the  juvenile  for all the purposes of this Act. 9. Jurisdiction and procedure (1) An application for an  adoption order  may be made to the High  Court  or, at the option of the applicant and subject to any rules made under this section, to any Juvenile  Court  within the jurisdiction of which the applicant or the infant resides at the date of the application. (2) The Chief Justice may, by legislative instrument, make rules in regard to any matter to be prescribed under this Act and dealing generally with all matters of procedure and incidental matters arising out of this Act or for carrying this Act into effect. (3) Rules under this section shall provide— (a) for the proceedings to be held otherwise than in open court except in such exceptional circumstances as may be provided for by the rules; (b) for the admission of documentary evidence of any consent required under section  3  or section  4  of this Act; (c) for requiring the  Director  to represent the interests of the  juvenile  in any proceedings with respect to an  adoption order  or an interim order; (d) for requiring the  Director  to prepare for the consideration of the  Court  on an application for an  adoption order  a report for the assistance of the  Court  in determining whether the order  will  be for the welfare of the  juvenile . 10. Appeals (1) On any decision by a Juvenile  Court  on an application for the making of an  adoption order , other than a decision to postpone the application and make an interim order, any person aggrieved may, subject to rules of court and subject to the provisions of section 35 of the Courts Act, 1960 (C.A. 9), appeal to the High  Court . (2) On any decision of the High  Court  (sitting in its original jurisdiction) on an application for an  adoption order  any person aggrieved may appeal to the Supreme  Court . 11. Rights and duties of parents and other persons (1) Upon an  adoption order  being made— (a) all rights, duties, obligations and liabilities, including any arising under customary law, of the parents of the  juvenile , or of any other person, in relation to the future custody, maintenance and education of the  juvenile  (including all rights to appoint a guardian and to consent or give notice of dissent to marriage) shall be extinguished; and (b) there shall vest in, and be exercisable by and enforceable against, the adopter all such rights, duties, obligations and liabilities in relation to the future custody, maintenance and education of the  juvenile  as would vest in him if the  juvenile  were a child born to the adopter in lawful marriage. (2) In respect of custody, maintenance and education the  juvenile  shall stand to the adopter exclusively in the position of a child born to the adopter in lawful marriage. (3) In a case where a man and his wife are the adopters, they shall in respect of the custody, maintenance and education of the  juvenile , and for the purpose of the jurisdiction of any  Court  to make orders as to the custody and maintenance of and rights of access to the  juvenile , stand to each other and to the  juvenile  in the same relation as they would have stood if they had been the lawful  father  and mother of the  juvenile  and the  juvenile  shall stand to them respectively in the same relation as to a lawful  father  and mother respectively.

Title: Applicant v 1st Respondent and 2nd Respondent (A6/16/20) [2025] GHADC 291 (24 March 2025)

Source: https://ghalii.org/akn/gh/judgment/ghadc/2025/291/eng@2025-03-24

Text: A custody dispute arose after a young child had been cared for by the applicant since 2018 following the mother’s mental-health problems and the death of the child’s initial caregiver. The applicant applied for guardianship and custody under the Children’s Act. The tribunal found it had jurisdiction under sections 43 and 45 of the Children’s Act but not under the High Court provision cited by the applicant. Evidence including a psychiatric report and a social enquiry established that the biological mother has significant mental-health challenges and is not presently competent to care for the child. The child, now ten, had lived with the applicant for years and expressed a desire to remain with her. Applying the best-interest factors in section 45(2)—age, parental preference tempered by fitness, the child’s views, and the need for continuity—the tribunal concluded custody with the applicant was in the child’s best interests. The biological mother was nonetheless granted reasonable supervised access. The tribunal rejected the first respondent’s non-parental claim and noted adverse conduct and failure to pursue adoption.

Issues:
- Whether the Family Tribunal has jurisdiction to determine the custody application under the Children’s Act and/or Courts Act.
- In the best interest of the child, who should be awarded custody of the child?
- Whether the biological mother’s mental state renders her unfit for custody despite presumptive parental preference.
- What weight should be given to the child’s views, continuity of care, and conduct of other claimants (including alleged kidnapping and adoption inaction) in awarding custody?
- Whether supervised access should be granted to the biological mother and on what terms?

Held:
- The Family Tribunal has jurisdiction to determine custody under sections 43 and 45 of the Children’s Act 1998 (Act 560), but not under section 18 of the Courts Act 1993, which relates to the High Court. The tribunal therefore limited its consideration to custody issues under the Children’s Act.
- The tribunal held that although a biological parent ordinarily has the stronger claim to custody, the second respondent (the biological mother) was not a competent person to be awarded custody due to her demonstrated mental health challenges, supported by psychiatric and social enquiry reports.
- Applying the best-interests factors in section 45(2) of the Children’s Act—including the child’s age, the child’s independently expressed wishes, and the need for continuity in care—the tribunal found the applicant (who had cared for the child since 2018) to be the person best suited to have custody.
- The tribunal rejected the first respondent’s claim to any special custodial entitlement based on familial feelings or ‘better title,’ noting that non-parents have no presumptive right to custody; the first respondent’s conduct (including a prior kidnapping conviction) and failure to pursue adoption weighed against her claim.
- The tribunal ordered that the applicant be granted custody and that the biological mother be granted reasonable supervised access, to be provided at her or the child’s request and supervised as suggested by medical officers.

Title: Forson v Forson (A4/05/2024) [2025] GHADC 65 (22 January 2025)

Source: https://ghalii.org/akn/gh/judgment/ghadc/2025/65/eng@2025-01-22

Text: The petitioner, married in 2010 and mother of two, petitioned for dissolution in November 2023 citing lack of maintenance, desertion and threats to life. The respondent denied the allegations, counter-claimed the petitioner’s unreasonable behaviour and alleged she left the matrimonial home in December 2022. Both parties filed witness statements and did not produce documentary proof beyond the marriage certificate; contested claims of assault (a scissors incident) lacked corroborating evidence. The court applied the Matrimonial Causes Act (Act 367), finding that failure to maintain and the alleged insulting/assaultive conduct amounted to unreasonable behaviour sufficient to show the marriage had broken down beyond reconciliation. Desertion was not established. The parties had executed terms of settlement which the court adopted as a consent judgment for ancillary reliefs. The court dissolved the marriage on 22 January 2025 and ordered custody to the petitioner with respondent access on weekends and vacations, respondent to pay GHS 400 monthly for the children (reviewed upward 20% annually), respondent to meet school fees, and both parents to equally share clothing, health and incidental expenses.

Issues:
- Whether the marriage had broken down beyond reconciliation within the meaning of Section 1(2) of the Matrimonial Causes Act, 1971 (Act 367)?
- Whether allegations of unreasonable behaviour and failure to maintain established a ground for dissolution?
- Whether the petitioner proved desertion as a ground for dissolution?
- Whether the parties’ executed terms of settlement should be adopted by the court as a consent judgment for ancillary reliefs?
- What custody, maintenance and ancillary orders are appropriate in the circumstances?

Held:
- The court held that the marriage had broken down beyond reconciliation. The evidence (witness statements, petition and answer) established unreasonable behaviour and failure to maintain which, singly or cumulatively, satisfied the statutory ground for dissolution under the Matrimonial Causes Act.
- The court found that desertion was not proved by the petitioner. Although the parties had been living separately since 2022 and reconciliation efforts failed, the facts as presented did not establish desertion as a separate ground.
- The court accepted and adopted the parties’ filed terms of settlement as a consent judgment for ancillary reliefs. Accordingly, custody, maintenance and other ancillary matters were ordered in accordance with those agreed terms.

Title: Ansah v Ansah ([1982-83] GLR 1127) [1983] GHAHC 2 (17 March 1983)

Source: https://ghalii.org/akn/gh/judgment/ghahc/1983/2/eng@1983-03-17

Text: The applicant (wife) petitioned for divorce alleging cruelty and desertion culminating in breakdown beyond reconciliation. The parties had married in 1963 and lived together until marital relations deteriorated after accusations, taunts and incidents of indignity by the respondent (a minister). The applicant left the matrimonial home in September 1972. A reconciliation meeting took place in November 1972, but the parties did not resume cohabitation. The applicant’s earlier petition was struck out for want of prosecution; she filed again in 1975. The respondent argued the earlier reconciliation barred the later petition. The court applied s.2(1)(b) and s.4 of the Matrimonial Causes Act, 1971 (Act 367), adopting an objective test for whether a spouse can reasonably be expected to live with the other. Finding the respondent’s conduct sufficiently serious, and that no post-reconciliation cohabitation restored the marriage, the court dissolved the marriage. On custody, the court emphasized the children’s best interests, considered parental conduct and the post-separation life-pattern, and refused the applicant’s custody claim while permitting existing living arrangements to continue. No order as to costs was made.

Issues:
- Whether the respondent's conduct amounted to such unreasonable behaviour that the applicant could not reasonably be expected to live with the respondent under s.2(1)(b) of the Matrimonial Causes Act, 1971 (Act 367).
- Whether an alleged reconciliation effected in November 1972 barred the applicant from petitioning for divorce based on prior unreasonable behaviour, having regard to s.4 of Act 367.
- What factors should govern custody orders in divorce proceedings and whether the applicant should be granted custody of the two children.

Held:
- The court held that the respondent had behaved towards the applicant in such a way that the applicant could not reasonably be expected to live with him, applying an objective test under s.2(1)(b) of Act 367; the conduct complained of was sufficiently serious (taunts, indignities, the ‘white handkerchief’ incident, scandalous proceedings) to justify dissolution of the marriage.
- The court held that the reconciliation promoted in November 1972 did not bar the applicant from bringing the 1975 petition. Section 4 of Act 367 requires disregard of short cohabitation periods; here there was no cohabitation after the reconciliation and the parties continued to live apart, so the petition was competent.
- On custody, the court held that the child's welfare is paramount but that the court must make orders reasonable and beneficial to the children; parental conduct and the life-pattern established since cessation of cohabitation are important considerations. The applicant’s custody claim was refused with arrangements made for the children to remain where settled.
response:
Yes, you can adopt your sister's child, but it has to go through a court — you can't simply take the child in as your own.

Because you are a relative, **Section 2 of the Adoption Act, 1962** gives you an easier path: you must be at least 21 years old (someone unrelated would need to be 25 and at least 21 years older than the child). Both you and the child must live in Ghana, the child must have been in your care for at least three months before the order is made, and you must tell the Director of Social Welfare at least three months before you apply. The child must be under 17 years old.

Your sister and the child's father must both agree to the adoption, unless the court decides their agreement can be dropped — for example, if they abandoned or neglected the child (**Section 3**). You then apply to the High Court or a Juvenile Court (**Section 9**), and these hearings are usually held privately, not in open court.

Other parts of the Act also matter: the court must be satisfied the adoption is for the child's welfare, and once the order is made the child becomes legally yours as if born to you, while your sister's parental rights end. I couldn't find the actual application forms or filing rules in my documents, so ask the court registry or a lawyer about those.

One caution: in **Applicant v 1st Respondent and 2nd Respondent**, the tribunal noted a non-parent who had cared for a child for years but never pursued adoption — caring for a child does not by itself give you legal rights over them.

This is general information based on the documents I have, not formal legal advice. For your specific case, please speak to a lawyer or Legal Aid Ghana.

Text: (1) Subject to the provisions of subsection  (2)  of section  25  and of section  28 , no order against a tenant for the recovery of the possession of, or for the ejectment from, any premises shall be made or given by the appropriate Rent Magistrate, or any other Judge of a court of competent jurisdiction in accordance with the provisions of any other enactment for the time being in force, except in any of the following circumstances:— (a) where any rent lawfully due from the  tenant  has not been paid or tendered within one month after the date on which it became lawfully due; (b) where any obligation of the tenancy, other than that specified in paragraph  (a) , so far as such obligation is consistent with the provisions of this Act, has been broken or not performed; (c) where the  tenant  or any person residing with him has been guilty of conduct which is a nuisance or an annoyance to adjoining occupiers; (d) where the  tenant  or any person residing with him has been convicted of using the  premises  or allowing the  premises  to be used for an immoral or illegal purpose; (e) where the condition of the  premises  has in the opinion of such Magistrate or Judge deteriorated owing to acts of waste by, or the neglect or default of, the  tenant  or any person residing with him; (f) where the  tenant  has given notice of his intention to quit in writing and in consequence of such notice the  landlord  has contracted to sell or  let  the  premises  or has taken any other steps as a result of which he would, in the opinion of such Magistrate or Judge, be seriously prejudiced if he could not obtain possession; (g) where the  premises  are reasonably required by the  landlord  for personal occupation as a dwelling house by himself, a member of his family or any person in his whole time employment, such  premises  being constructed to be used as a dwelling house, so, however, that— (i) the circumstance that the  premises  are reasonably required by the  landlord  for personal occupation by someone in his employ shall not be a sufficient circumstance if the Magistrate or Judge is not satisfied that such  landlord  usually provides  premises  for occupation by an employee of the class to which that employee belongs, and (ii) no such order shall be made if the Magistrate or Judge is satisfied having regard to all the circumstances of the case, including any alternative accommodation available for the person for whose occupation the  premises  are so required or for the  tenant , that greater hardship would be caused by granting the order than by refusing it; (h) where the  lease  has expired and the  premises  are reasonably required by the  landlord  to be used by him for his own business purposes, such  premises  being constructed to be used as such, if the  landlord  has given not less than six months' written notice to the  tenant  of his intention to apply for an order for the recovery of the possession of, or the ejectment from, the  premises ; (i) where the  lease  has expired and the  tenant  is a  statutory tenant  and the  landlord — (i) intends to pull down the  premises  and construct new  premises , (ii) intends to remodel the  premises  and the remodelling cannot be carried out with the  tenant  in occupation, or (iii) requires possession of the  premises  to carry out a scheme of re-development, if the  landlord  has given not less than six months' written notice to the  tenant  of his intention to apply for an order for the recovery of the possession of, or the ejectment from, the  premises , so, however, that— (aa) the Magistrate or Judge may, on making or giving an order under this paragraph, make it a condition that if the  landlord  fails to carry out his intention within such period as may be allowed by such Magistrate or Judge the  landlord  shall reinstate the former  tenant  as a  statutory tenant  at the same rent as that formerly payable or pay to the  tenant  such compensation as the Magistrate or Judge may consider reasonable, (ab) the Magistrate or Judge shall cause a copy of such order to be served on the appropriate Rent Officer for the area where the  premises  are situated and such officer shall take such proceedings as are necessary to ensure compliance with the terms of the order, and (ac) the making or giving of an order under this paragraph in the circumstances specified in paragraph  (i) (ii)  of this subsection shall be subject to any option of the tenant to acquire under the provisions of section  18 , a new statutory tenancy of any premises remodelled to which such an order relates; (j) where the  premises  were  let  to the  tenant  by reason of his employment in the service of the  landlord  and such employment has ceased; and (k) where the  landlord  was personally in occupation of the  premises  and has  let  the  premises  substantially furnished for a term during his absence from Ghana or that area of Ghana in which the  premises  are situated and has returned and requires the re-occupation of the  premises  for himself, so, however, that no order granting the possession of, or the ejectment from, the  premises  shall be granted on or after the commencement of this Act unless the  lease  is in writing and sets out that the  lease  has been granted for a term during the absence of the  landlord  from Ghana or such area. (2) Subsection  (1)  of this section shall not apply to— (a) proceedings by a person claiming under a title adverse and superior to that under which the original tenancy by virtue of which the  tenant  became entitled to retain possession was derived; or (b) proceedings against a derivative  landlord ; or (c) proceedings by or on behalf of the Republic. (3) The Magistrate or Judge making or giving any order or judgment for the recovery of the possession of any  premises  or for the ejectment of a  tenant  therefrom may stay or suspend execution of any such order or judgment or postpone the date of possession for such period or periods as the Magistrate or Judge thinks fit and subject to such conditions, if any, in regard to payment by the  tenant  of arrears of rent, mesne profits and such other sums as the Magistrate or Judge thinks fit and if such conditions are complied with, the Magistrate or Judge may discharge or rescind such order or judgment. (4) An order for recovery of possession or ejectment given or made under the provisions of paragraph (g) of subsection  (1)  shall state in full the name of the person who is to occupy the premises. (5) An order or judgment against a  tenant  for the recovery of the possession of any  premises  or ejectment therefrom made or given under the provisions of this section or of subsection (2) of section  25  shall not affect the right of any sub-tenant to whom the premises or any part thereof were lawfully sub-let before proceedings for recovery of possession or ejectment were commenced, to retain possession under this section, and every such order or judgment shall declare whether it shall be enforced against a sub-tenant or not. (6) Any sub- tenant  against whom an order or judgment is not enforceable shall, if he remains in possession after notice of the order or judgment, cease to be a sub- tenant  of the  tenant  and become a  tenant  of the  landlord . (7) A  landlord  in whose favour an order for recovery of the possession of, or the ejectment from,  premises  on any of the grounds specified in paragraph  (g) , (h) or  (k)  of subsection  (1)  has been made or given shall not, within two years from the date of the order, let such premises or any part thereof without an order of the appropriate Rent Magistrate, except, in the case of an order on grounds specified in the said paragraph  (g) , to the person or persons for whom the premises were stated to be required in the proceedings in which such recovery or ejectment was obtained.

Title: Rent Act, 1963

Source: https://ghalii.org/akn/gh/act/1963/220/eng@1971-12-31#part_VII

Text: 25. Offences (1) Every person who, in respect of any  premises — (a) demands or receives more than the  recoverable rent  for such  premises  notwithstanding any  lease  to the contrary; (b) demands or receives any consideration, whether in money or in kind or in any other manner whatsoever and whether by way of rent, fine, premium or otherwise, for the grant, renewal, continuance or assignment of any tenancy; (c) being or acting as an agent or broker or go-between demands or receives for his services in connection with the procuring of any grant, renewal, continuance or assignment of a tenancy, any consideration which exceeds five  per centum  of the  recoverable rent  for one year of such  premises ; (d) where the purchase or hire of any furniture, fittings, fixtures, or other articles is required by him as a condition for the grant, renewal, continuance or assignment of any tenancy, demands or receives any price or consideration for such purchase or hire in excess of a reasonable price or consideration therefor; (e) enters into or carries out any fictitious or artificial agreement which has the effect of attempting to defeat the objects of this Act; (f) being a  landlord  fails to furnish any information he is required to furnish by or under this Act; (g) being a  landlord  of any  premises  ejects a  tenant  of such  premises  for failing to pay more than the  recoverable rent  of the  premises ; (h) being a  landlord  and having remodelled  premises  after obtaining possession under the provisions of paragraph (i) of subsection (1) of section  17  fails to comply with the requirements of section  18 ; or (i) contravenes any other provisions of the Act, shall be guilty of an offence and shall upon conviction by the  appropriate Rent Magistrate  be liable to a fine not exceeding one hundred pounds or to imprisonment for a term not exceeding six months or to both such fine and imprisonment. (2) Upon the hearing of a charge alleging the contravention of the provisions of subsection  (1) , it shall be lawful for the Magistrate, in addition to imposing a fine if the accused is convicted, to order the accused to pay the tenant such one or more of the following sums as may be appropriate to the case:— (a) any sum received in excess of the rent lawfully recoverable; (b) the amount or value of the consideration paid in contravention of the provisions of paragraph (b) or (c) of subsection  (1) ; and (c) the amount by which the price or consideration for such purchase or hire referred to in paragraph (d) of subsection  (1)  exceeds a reasonable price or consideration. Upon such hearing the Magistrate may, also if the accused is a principal  tenant  order his ejectment. (3) Nothing in this section contained shall prejudice the right of any person to recover by civil action any such sums as the Magistrate may order to be paid under subsection  (2) . (4) Where there is any such change of circumstances in a tenancy as the following, that is to say, any diminution of the rights of the  tenant  to use accommodation in common with others which renders the letting less favourable to the  tenant  without a corresponding reduction in rent, there shall be deemed to have been an increase in rent. (5) Any person who as a condition of the grant, renewal or continuance of a tenancy demands in the case of a monthly or shorter tenancy, the payment in advance of more than a month's rent or in the case of a tenancy exceeding six months, the payment in advance of more than six months rent shall be guilty of an offence and shall upon conviction by the  appropriate Rent Magistrate  be liable to a fine not exceeding one hundred pounds. (6) Notwithstanding anything in subsection  (1) , an assignor may, if apart from this section he would be entitled so to do, require the payment by the assignee— (a) of so much of any outgoings discharged by the assignor as is referable to any period after the assignment takes effect; (b) of a sum not exceeding the amount of any expenditure reasonably incurred by the assignor in carrying out any structural alteration of the  premises  or in providing or improving fixtures, therein, being fixtures which as against the  landlord  he is not entitled to remove; (c) where the assignor became a  tenant  of the  premises  by virtue of an assignment of the tenancy thereof, of a sum not exceeding any reasonable amount paid by him to his assignor in respect of expenditure incurred by that assignor, or by any previous assignor of the tenancy, in carrying out any such alteration or in providing or improving any such fixtures as are mentioned in paragraph  (b)  of this subsection; or (d) where the  premises  or any part thereof are used as a shop or office, or for business, trade or professional purposes, of a reasonable amount in respect of any goodwill of the business, trade or profession, being goodwill transferred to the assignee in connection with the assignment or accruing to him in consequence thereof. 26. Offences by agents and servants (1) Where an offence which may be committed by a  landlord  or  tenant  under this Act has in fact been committed by his agent or servant, such agent or servant shall be liable to the like penalty as if he were the  landlord  or  tenant , as the case may be. (2) Any  landlord  or  tenant , who would have been guilty of an offence under the provisions of this Act for anything done or omitted to be done by him personally, shall be guilty of such offence if such thing has been done or omitted by his agent or servant, unless he proves that he took reasonable precautions to prevent the doing or omission of such thing. 27. Offences for inducing  tenant  to quit (1) Every person who shall do any act whatsoever, or refrain from doing anything which the conditions of the tenancy require him to do, with intent to compel the lessee of any  premises  to give up possession thereof shall be guilty of an offence and shall on conviction by the  appropriate Rent Magistrate , be liable to a fine not exceeding fifty pounds. (2) Upon the hearing of a charge alleging the contravention of the provisions of subsection  (1) , it shall be lawful for the Magistrate if the accused is convicted and in addition to imposing a fine, to order the accused to pay to the lessee of the premises, such sum as may appear to the Magistrate reasonable to compensate the lessee for any costs, damages, or loss or inconvenience sustained by him by reason of such act or omission and, if he so thinks fit, make an order reinstating the lessee in such premises. 28. Statutory  tenant  prohibited from demanding premium (1) If a  statutory tenant  demands or receives the payment of any fine or premium or any other consideration for giving up possession of  premises  to the  landlord  or to any other person with or without the knowledge or approval of the  landlord , such  tenant  shall be guilty of an offence and shall be liable on conviction by the  appropriate Rent Magistrate  to imprisonment for a term not exceeding three months or a fine not exceeding one hundred pounds, or to both such imprisonment and fine. For the purposes of this section the demanding or receiving of a price or consideration for any furniture, fittings, fixtures or other articles in excess of a reasonable price or consideration therefor shall be deemed to be the demanding or receiving of a premium. (2) Upon the hearing of a charge alleging the contravention of the provisions of subsection  (1) , it shall be lawful for the Magistrate upon conviction of the accused and in addition to imposing a fine— (a) to order the accused to pay the person from whom such fine, premium or other consideration has been received the amount of such fine, premium or other consideration wrongfully received, including the amount by which the price or consideration paid for any furniture, fittings, fixtures or other articles exceeds the reasonable value thereof; and (b) to order the ejectment of the  tenant . 29. Obligations of statutory tenants (1) A  statutory tenant  shall, so long as he retains possession, hold the  premises  of the  landlord  upon the following terms and conditions, namely— (a) he shall hold as a  tenant  from month to month, and, subject thereto, shall observe and be entitled to the benefit of all the terms and conditions of his original tenancy, as the case may be, so far as the same are consistent with the provisions of this Act, so, however, that, in the case of a  tenant  who has become a  statutory tenant  by reason of the provisions of paragraph (c) of the definition of “ statutory tenant ” in section  36 , he shall in addition hold the premises subject to any restrictive covenants contained in the terms and conditions of the lease between the landlord and the principal tenant; (b) his tenancy shall be determinable by him by such notice as would have been required by law to determine a monthly tenancy of the  premises  containing no express provision for determination thereof; and (c) he shall be subject to all the rights and powers conferred upon a  landlord  under and by virtue of any provision of law relating to distress for arrears of rent. 30. Furnished  premises Where  premises  are  let  together with furniture or fixtures the combined  recoverable rent  of  premises  and furniture or fixtures shall be the rent at which the  premises  were  let  with furniture or fixtures on the first day of July, 1960, or, where the  premises  were not so  let  on that date the rent at which they were last so  let  before that date, or, in the case of  premises  which were first so  let  after that date the  recoverable rent  of the  premises   let  unfurnished and without fixtures with the addition per month of one-sixtieth of the true value of the furniture or fixtures at the date of the commencement of the tenancy: Provided that if a combined  recoverable rent  has been assessed under this Act, such rent shall be the combined  recoverable rent . 31. Rates in relation to rents Nothing in this Act shall be so construed as to prevent a  landlord  from collecting from his  tenant  the rates for the time being payable in respect of any  premises , or such apportioned sum as shall properly be attributable to such  premises  in respect of rates, if the obligation of paying rates in respect of such  premises  was assumed by the  tenant  under the terms of the  lease , or when the  recoverable rent  therefor has been assessed under this Act, if the obligation of payment of rates was stated in the order assessing such rent to be payable by the  tenant . 32. Excess rent paid in advance Where a  recoverable rent  applies under this Act and prior to the commencement of this Act a  landlord  has received a payment of rent in advance for periods of the tenancy which have not commenced on the date on which such rent commenced to apply, any such excess of rent shall be applied by the  landlord  as the rent for the next succeeding periods until out of the total moneys paid in advance the  landlord  retains only an amount equal to the  recoverable rent  for the period for which rent may lawfully be demanded in advance: Provided that where a tenancy is determined by any means prior to such application by the  landlord  of the whole of such excess, the balance unapplied may be recovered from the  landlord  by the  tenant  as if it were a debt due from the  landlord  to the  tenant . 33. Receipt for rent to be supplied At the time of payment to a  landlord  of any sum in respect of rent for  premises , or of rent for  premises  and for the use of furniture or fixtures, such  landlord  shall provide the person making such payment with a receipt in writing, duly stamped if a stamp is required under any other enactment for the time being in force, specifying the  premises  in respect of which the rent is paid, whether the  premises  are furnished or unfurnished, the amount paid, the period in respect of which the payment is made and the name of the  tenant .

Title: Osekre v Saah [1967] GHAHC 38 (14 March 1967)

Source: https://ghalii.org/akn/gh/judgment/ghahc/1967/38/eng@1967-03-14

Text: The landlord let premises on a monthly tenancy to a tenant who, without the landlord’s written consent, let part of the premises to the defendant. After the original tenant fell into arrears and gave up possession on notice to quit, the defendant remained in occupation and sought to remain via a rent office inquiry. The rent officer required the landlord to issue a receipt for rent paid by the defendant; the landlord complied unwillingly. The court considered whether the occupant was a lawful sub‑tenant and whether the receipt and payment created a new tenancy. Applying section 22(1) of the Rent Act 1963, the court held that sub‑letting without written consent was unlawful and so the occupant could not be a sub‑tenant. The court further held that accepting rent and issuing a receipt after tenancy had been terminated did not create a new tenancy absent evidence of mutual intention to that effect. The unlawful occupation was therefore trespass; the landlord was awarded N¢ 988 damages, an order for possession forthwith, and costs of N¢ 200.

Issues:
- Whether a sub‑letting of premises under a monthly tenancy without the landlord’s written consent is lawful under section 22(1) of the Rent Act, 1963 (Act 220).
- Whether a person who occupies premises under an unlawful sub‑letting can be regarded as a tenant within the meaning of section 36 of Act 220.
- Whether acceptance of rent and issuance of a receipt by the landlord (at the rent officer’s insistence) after notice to quit creates a new tenancy in favour of the occupant.
- What is the legal effect of payment of rent after termination of a tenancy by notice to quit—does such payment waive the notice or create a new tenancy?
- Whether the unlawful occupation constituted trespass entitling the landlord to damages and an order for recovery of possession.

Held:
- The court held that section 22(1) of the Rent Act, 1963 (Act 220) prohibits sub‑letting of premises let on a monthly (or shorter) tenancy without the landlord’s written consent; because no written consent was produced, the sub‑letting was unlawful and the person in occupation could not be regarded as a lawful sub‑tenant (Maley v. Fearn applied).
- The court held that acceptance of rent and issuance of a receipt after the original tenancy had been terminated by notice to quit does not, of itself, create a new tenancy. What matters is the quid animo (intention) of the parties; absent evidence of an intention to create a new tenancy, payment and receipt do not waive the notice or confer tenant status (Doe d. Cheny v. Batten and Clarke v. Grant applied).
- The court held that the combination of unlawful sub‑letting and the occupant’s refusal to give up possession after being asked to quit constituted trespass in tort. The landlord was entitled to damages for trespass, an order for recovery of possession, and costs.

Title: Tackie v Bannerman [1978] GHAHC 45 (4 April 1978)

Source: https://ghalii.org/akn/gh/judgment/ghahc/1978/45/eng@1978-04-04

Text: A landlord gave written notice to quit and, after the tenant held over, applied to a rent officer for recovery of possession under the Rent Act. The rent officer dismissed the complaint; the rent magistrate reversed that decision and ordered recovery of possession. On appeal the High Court considered four issues: requirement to prove title, compliance with regulation 18, necessity of a notice to quit before suing under s.17(1)(g), and the rent officer’s jurisdiction. The court held that the tenant was estopped from denying the landlord’s status where admitted into possession, so proof of title was irrelevant. It followed precedent that regulation 18 is not a condition precedent to s.17(1)(g) proceedings. The court further held that s.17(1)(g) does not mandate prior service of a notice to quit as a condition of suit. Crucially, the court concluded that a rent officer lacks jurisdiction under s.5(1)(b) to hear or determine recovery of possession/ejectment claims, which are reserved for the rent magistrate or courts; accordingly the lower decision was set aside and costs awarded.

Issues:
- Whether a landlord must prove legal title to premises to bring an action under section 17(1)(g) of the Rent Act.
- Whether compliance with regulation 18 of the Rent Regulations (L.I. 369) is a condition precedent to maintaining an action under section 17(1)(g).
- Whether service of a notice to quit is mandatorily required before commencing proceedings under section 17(1)(g).
- Whether a rent officer has jurisdiction under section 5(1)(b) of the Rent Act, 1963 (Act 220) to investigate or decide complaints for recovery of possession or ejectment.

Held:
- The court held that a landlord need not prove legal title to the premises in order to bring an action under section 17(1)(g); where the tenant admits being let into possession by the claimant, the tenant is estopped from denying the landlord’s status.
- The court held that compliance with regulation 18 of the Rent Regulations (L.I. 369) is not a condition precedent to an action under section 17(1)(g), endorsing Alameddine Bros. v. Paterson Zochonis.
- The court held that section 17(1)(g) does not require service of a notice to quit as a precondition to instituting proceedings; a notice may determine a tenancy, but a tenant who holds over becomes a statutory tenant and may be sued under s.17(1)(g).
- The court held that a rent officer has no jurisdiction to entertain or determine complaints for recovery of possession or ejectment under section 5(1)(b); such powers are reserved to the rent magistrate (and courts) under section 6(d) and section 17, and section 5 should not be construed to include s.17 actions.

Title: Alameddine Brothers v Paterson Zochonis And Co., Ltd. [1971] GHACA 2 (19 July 1971)

Source: https://ghalii.org/akn/gh/judgment/ghaca/1971/2/eng@1971-07-19

Text: The appellants occupied shop premises under an oral letting originally expressed as payable monthly; the rent was reduced following assessment and paid during the tenancy. The landlord served an initial one‑month notice and later a six‑month notice under section 17(1)(h) of the Rent Act, seeking possession because the premises were required for its business expansion. At trial the appellants alleged that rent had later been paid quarterly and then half‑yearly, and challenged the validity of the notices. The magistrate and High Court found the tenancy remained monthly and that the premises were reasonably required by the landlord. On further appeal the Court of Appeal held that any alleged variation of the tenancy had to be proved by the party asserting it; no such evidence was forthcoming, and payments in advance did not alter a tenancy whose rent was expressed monthly. The court refused to entertain a new argument about the technical form of notice not raised earlier, observed that English rules on termination need not control Ghanaian practice and invoked the Interpretation Act for reckoning months, and upheld the magistrate’s factual finding that the premises were reasonably required. The appeal was dismissed.

Issues:
- Whether the demand for quarterly and later half‑yearly rent in advance operated to vary an original monthly tenancy.
- Whether it was lawful to demand more than one month’s rent in advance from a monthly tenant under section 25(5) of the Rent Act, 1963 (Act 220).
- Whether a notice to quit given on a particular day is invalid for not expiring at the end of a periodic month from the commencement of the tenancy.
- Whether English rules on the termination of weekly and monthly tenancies should be applied in Ghana.
- Whether premises are ‘reasonably required’ by a landlord for business purposes under section 17(1)(h) of the Rent Act is a question of fact.
- Whether an appellant may raise on further appeal an issue of fact or law that was not raised at trial or on earlier appeal.

Held:
- The court held that the parties admitted the original letting was on a monthly basis and, absent proof of a lawful variation, demands for quarterly or half‑yearly rent in advance would contravene section 25(5) of the Rent Act and thus could not alter the tenancy’s monthly character.
- The burden of proving any variation of the original monthly tenancy lay on the party alleging it. No evidence was produced to establish an agreement converting the tenancy into a half‑yearly or yearly tenancy; payment in advance, even if made for convenience, did not change the legal nature of a tenancy where the rent was expressed as payable monthly (Carroll v. Andrews applied).
- The point that a notice must terminate at the end of a periodic month (an English rule) was not open to the appellants because it had not been raised before the trial court or the High Court; an appellate court will not permit a new factual/legal point to be raised for the first time on further appeal (Khoury v. Teymani dictum applied).
- The English rules on termination of periodic tenancies developed for English conditions may not be appropriate in Ghana; the court referred to the Interpretation Act s.23(2) as a local guideline for reckoning months and indicated mutual reciprocity between landlords and tenants in giving notice calculated accordingly.
- Whether premises are reasonably required by the landlord under section 17(1)(h) is a question of fact. The magistrate’s finding that the landlord reasonably required the premises for business (to expand operations) was a clear factual finding and was not successfully impugned on appeal.

No, your landlord no get right to just tell you make you comot — not like dat, without the law.

Under **Section 17(1) of the Rent Act, 1963**, no order for ejectment against a tenant fit be made at all unless the Rent Magistrate (the special court wey dey handle rent matters) make that order, and only for certain reasons — like if you no pay rent wey pass one month, or if the landlord really need the place for himself to live in.

The matter no be only about notice. As the case of **Tackie v Bannerman** show, even where notice to quit no be required, the landlord still must go to the Rent Magistrate to get possession — a rent officer no get power to order say make you comot. And if you hold over after notice, you become what dem call a statutory tenant, wey dem must sue properly before you comot.

Again, **Section 27 of the Rent Act, 1963** make am an offence for anybody to do any act to force a tenant to give up possession — the Magistrate fit fine the landlord and even put you back inside the house.

So no pack your things yet. Go see Legal Aid Ghana or a lawyer quick so dem fit advise you well.
